strengths: The paper develops a rigorous measure-theoretic framework that connects finite-batch InfoNCE to deterministic population energies, with both value and gradient consistency established under clearly stated regularity assumptions (Thms. 3.1, 4.1), which is more than the usual static-optimum characterization found in prior variational analyses.

The central conceptual contribution is convincing: the unimodal/multimodal bifurcation, where unimodal InfoNCE yields a strictly convex intrinsic energy with a unique Gibbs equilibrium (entropy as a tie-breaker within the alignment basin), while symmetric multimodal InfoNCE induces a negative symmetric KL divergence coupling that acts as a population-level barrier and structurally sustains the modality gap. This offers a mechanistic account of a well-known empirical phenomenon (Liang et al., 2022).

The technical machinery is careful and mostly self-contained: the sharp-diagonal-peak smoothing lemma (B.3), the KDE-bias bounds (Thms. 3.2, 4.2), and the extremal barrier best-response construction (Prop. 4.1, Cor. B.2) are done with genuine rigor, including honest treatment of density floors and positivity assumptions (App. A.3).

The experimental validation is well-matched to the theory: large-batch gradient alignment across two critic regimes, Gibbs-concentration of a particle surrogate, controlled latent-misalignment synthetic experiments isolating the gap mechanism, and a real-data interventional experiment (same-category caption corruption on MS-COCO fine-tuning) that shows widening cross-modal discrepancy even when coarse semantics are preserved — supporting the paper's claim that pairwise alignment alone does not control marginal geometry.

Limitations are discussed honestly and precisely (App. F.1): asymptotic regimes (N→∞, τ→0+), density floors, constant kernel volume, and the gap between objective geometry and optimization trajectories are all flagged rather than glossed over.
weaknesses: The unimodal results rest on fairly classical variational facts (a linear potential plus negative entropy yields a Gibbs measure; kernel smoothing converges to the true density), so the novel content there is mainly the connection machinery to InfoNCE dynamics rather than the intrinsic characterization itself.

Several bridging steps rely on strong assumptions that disconnect the theory from practical training: compact parameter spaces with uniform Jacobian bounds, constant kernel volume (only exactly valid on homogeneous manifolds), a sharp diagonal peak regime, and an expressivity assumption (Asm. B.1) needed for the 'parametric inheritance' claims. The gap between the asymptotic idealization and realistic batch sizes/temperatures is acknowledged but only partially bridged (Fig. 3 shows alignment at moderate N, yet the multimodal barrier predictions are only tested qualitatively).

The main practical conclusion — that pairwise alignment is insufficient to control cross-modal marginal structure — is partly anticipated by the alignment–uniformity literature and existing modality-gap analyses; the paper positions itself as complementary, but the incremental conceptual novelty over Calder & Lee (2025)-style variational analyses is not fully delineated beyond the gradient-consistency and bifurcation framing.

The MS-COCO interventional experiment fine-tunes only projection heads on frozen backbones, so the claim that the observed gap growth reflects objective-induced geometry rather than capacity/architecture adaptation is suggestive but not conclusively established; only two backbones are tested.
Reproducibility is decent (hyperparameters, seeds, and protocols are given in App. E), but no code release is explicitly confirmed; the 'project page' footnote appears truncated.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent measure-theoretic framework that connects finite-batch InfoNCE to deterministic population energies, with both value- and gradient-consistency statements (Thms. 3.1, 4.1) backed by detailed, largely careful proofs across ~40 pages of appendix material.

The intrinsic unimodal characterization (strictly convex free energy, unique Gibbs equilibrium, low-temperature concentration, Prop. 3.1–3.2) is clean, and the reinterpretation of 'uniformity' as entropy-driven dispersion within the alignment basin is a genuinely clarifying conceptual contribution beyond the alignment–uniformity view of Wang & Isola (2020).

The multimodal analysis identifies a concrete structural object — the negative symmetric KL coupling and the effective barrier potentials V1|2, V2|1 — that gives a testable mechanistic hypothesis for the modality gap, and the assumptions are honestly dissected (App. A.3, Remark 4.4).

The experimental section is well-matched to the theory at the synthetic level: gradient-consistency diagnostics (Fig. 3), a particle-based Gibbs-equilibrium validation (Fig. 7/2a), and a controlled misalignment sweep (Figs. 5, 8–10) with an interventional MS-COCO study (Fig. 6b, Tab. 2).
Limitations are discussed candidly in App. F.1, including the large-batch/low-temperature regime and the density-floor technicality.
weaknesses: The bridge from the intrinsic analysis to actual training is the weakest link and is not convincingly established. The consistency results (Thms. 3.1, 4.1) are pointwise in θ: they show convergence of loss/gradient values at each fixed θ, not uniform convergence over Θ. The repeated claim that large-batch InfoNCE 'follows gradient descent' on the deterministic energy therefore requires a uniformity argument (e.g., over the training trajectory) that the paper does not provide; Lemma B.1 bounds gradients but not the convergence of gradient differences uniformly.

The intrinsic multimodal 'bifurcation' (Prop. 4.1, Cor. B.2) rests on assumptions that strain credibility for real models: the coordinate best response is an extremal, spiky density concentrated on sublevel sets of V1|2 while flat at the density floor elsewhere, and the parametric inheritance corollary requires the encoder family to approximate such competitors. Smooth encoders generically cannot realize these densities, so the transfer of the 'barrier-driven co-adaptation' mechanism to practical CLIP training is speculative. Similarly, Theorems 3.2/4.2 require inf_z ρθ(z) ≥ ρ_θ > 0 — densities bounded away from zero everywhere — which is unrealistic for learned representations that effectively concentrate on low-dimensional structures.

The headline claim — that the modality gap is a structural property of the objective rather than an optimization artifact — is stronger than the evidence. The parametric energy J^Sym contains no negative KL term at finite temperature; the divergence coupling appears only in the intrinsic surrogate evaluated at fixed densities in the τ→0 limit. The synthetic experiments validate the surrogate directly (the unimodal experiment optimizes F_{τ,U} via a KDE surrogate, not InfoNCE), and the MS-COCO intervention enlarges the gap but does not discriminate the proposed mechanism from simpler explanations (weaker alignment, caption statistics, initialization cone effects à la Liang et al. 2022). The interventional study also only fine-tunes projection heads on frozen backbones, further limiting what it can test.

Much of the unimodal machinery is a re-derivation of standard results: the large-batch limit is an application of the law of large numbers to the softmax denominator, and the intrinsic convexity/Gibbs equilibrium is the textbook Gibbs variational principle. The genuinely novel content is concentrated in the multimodal surrogate analysis, whose practical relevance is, as noted above, the least well-supported part.

The relevance of the analyzed regime (N→∞, τ→0+, sharp diagonal kernels, constant kernel volume via Asm. 2.1) to practice is attenuated: the Euclidean/RBF regime does not even satisfy Asm. 2.1 without boundary corrections (App. A.1), and the quantitative gap between the asymptotic predictions and finite-batch, finite-temperature training is uncharacterized.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the notation is heavy (Table 1 is a full page), the 'Punchline' boxes assert strong claims ('modality gap a natural geometric consequence') that outrun the proven statements, and the project-page footnote is truncated with no URL, hindering verification of experimental details beyond the appendix.

The observational CLIP study (Fig. 6a, Tab. 2) establishes only that retrieval and marginal gap are not equivalent, which is already known qualitatively; it does not test any quantitative prediction of the theory (e.g., scaling of the gap with a controllable cross-modal compatibility parameter in a regime matching the theory's assumptions).

strengths: The paper develops a coherent measure-theoretic framework that connects finite-batch stochastic InfoNCE to deterministic population energies via large-batch value and gradient consistency (Thms. 3.1, 4.1), with proofs that are careful and largely self-contained (uniform gradient bounds, concentration of the negative partition sum, dominated-convergence arguments).

The unimodal analysis (strict convexity, unique Gibbs equilibrium, entropy as an 'entropy tie-breaker' within the alignment basin, low-temperature concentration in Prop. 3.2) is clean and gives a genuinely new, more precise reading of the alignment-uniformity decomposition of Wang & Isola (2020).

The multimodal analysis identifies a concrete structural mechanism — negative symmetric KL divergence coupling between modality marginals — that explains how pairwise alignment can coexist with a persistent modality gap, complementing prior descriptive (Liang et al. 2022) and identifiability-based accounts.

Experiments are well matched to the theory at three levels: synthetic verification of gradient consistency across critics and batch sizes, particle-based verification of Gibbs concentration, controlled misalignment experiments on S^1, and a real-data interventional study (caption corruption on MS-COCO) that supports the structural-gap prediction on pretrained OpenCLIP backbones.

Limitations are discussed honestly and specifically (finite-temperature/finite-batch gaps, density floors, constant kernel volume, objective geometry vs. optimization dynamics), and the appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail (seeds, hyperparameters, protocols).
weaknesses: The theory's regime is restrictive relative to practice: the constant kernel-volume assumption (Asm. 2.1) holds essentially only on compact homogeneous manifolds; the intrinsic equivalence requires the sharp-kernel, τ→0+ limit; and negative sampling is iid rather than in-batch. The paper acknowledges these, but they mean the core 'bifurcation' claims are verified only in an idealized regime.

The central multimodal characterization depends on the density-floor constraint ρ ≥ ρ̲; without it, the intrinsic functional is unbounded below and the 'barrier best response' is ill-posed (Remark 4.4 concedes this is a technical device). The argument that the floor faithfully proxies the interiority of kernel-smoothed densities at finite τ is plausible but heuristic, so the strongest claims about modality gaps as a 'structural consequence' rest on a partially justified idealization.

The bridge between intrinsic energies and parametric training (Thm. 3.2 / Thm. 4.2) requires both vanishing KDE mismatch (τ→0) and an expressivity assumption (Asm. B.1) that is stated but never verified or quantified for realistic encoder families, so the inheritance results are largely qualitative.

Empirical support for the multimodal mechanism, while consistent with predictions, is largely monotone-trend evidence (Figs. 2b, 5, 6, 12) without sharp quantitative predictions (e.g., predicted gap scaling in σ_mis or p) that would discriminate this theory from simpler accounts; the observational OpenCLIP study is correlational and the interventional study confirms only that degrading cross-modal compatibility widens the gap, which is fairly expected.

Presentation is dense and assumption-heavy; the headline framing ('geometric bifurcation') promises more than the technical content delivers, since the multimodal intrinsic problem admits no minimizer at all (infimum attained only at boundary spikes), which is a degenerate rather than bifurcating landscape.

Several claims of novelty relative to related work (e.g., vs. Calder & Lee 2025 variational analyses, and vs. modality-gap mechanistic accounts) are asserted as differences of 'emphasis' rather than substantiated by direct comparison or derived distinctions that could be tested.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent measure-theoretic framework connecting finite-batch InfoNCE to deterministic population energies, with genuine value- and gradient-consistency results (Thms. 3.1, 4.1) rather than value-only limits; this is a real technical contribution over prior landscape analyses.

The intrinsic analysis is clean and rigorous: strict convexity of the unimodal free energy, unique Gibbs equilibrium (Prop. 3.1), low-temperature concentration (Prop. 3.2), and the KL-decomposition identity underlying the sharp-kernel consistency results (Thms. 3.2, 4.2) are carefully proved in a substantial appendix, including uniform gradient bounds (Lems. B.1, B.2) and a vanishing-KDE lemma (Lem. B.3).

The multimodal 'bifurcation' story — negative symmetric KL coupling creating an occupied-mass barrier V12 = U12/τ + log ρ2 — offers a plausible population-level mechanism for the empirically known modality gap, complementing alignment–uniformity and double-ellipsoid accounts; the coordinate-extremal construction in Prop. D.1 is explicit and instructive.

The experimental program is well matched to the theory: synthetic tests of large-batch gradient consistency, Gibbs concentration, and controlled cross-modal misalignment, plus an MS-COCO study combining observational comparisons across OpenCLIP checkpoints with a controlled caption-corruption intervention (Fig. 6b) that goes beyond mere correlation.

Assumptions are transparent and honestly discussed (App. A), and the limitations section (App. G.1) candidly identifies the finite-temperature/finite-batch gap, the density-floor device, and the objective-vs-dynamics divide; there are no evident ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central quantitative results are pointwise (fixed θ, φ, fixed τ) and the link to actual training is indirect: parametric inheritance (Cors. E.1, E.2) requires an expressivity assumption (Eq. 65/69) that essentially presumes the encoder can attain the intrinsic optimum with vanishing error, making the strongest claims close to conditional restatements rather than predictions about learned encoders.

The multimodal 'barrier' geometry is characterized only through an infimum approached by extremal, boundary-concentrating densities (Prop. 4.1/D.1); no equilibrium, minimizer, or stability result is given for the multimodal functional, so the claimed sustained modality gap remains a landscape-level plausibility argument rather than a theorem about what SGD reaches. This gap is acknowledged but substantially weakens the headline claim.

A regime mismatch limits practical bite: the intrinsic bifurcation picture is a τ→0+ statement, while CLIP-style training uses fixed moderate τ; the paper does not quantify how large the barrier effect is at realistic temperatures, and the KDE-mismatch bounds require density floors and strict positivity assumptions whose behavior along training trajectories is unverified.

Assumption 2.1 (constant kernel volume) fails for the RBF kernel on generic compact Euclidean domains — one of the two regimes used in the gradient-consistency experiments — so part of the empirical validation exercises a setting the clean theory does not exactly cover (acknowledged in App. A.1 but not resolved).

The empirical evidence is largely confirmatory-of-consistency rather than discriminative: the synthetic experiments verify predictions that are close to tautological given the theorems, and the MS-COCO corruption study confounds weakened instance-level correspondence with changed task difficulty, so alternative explanations for the widening centroid gap are not fully excluded. No code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the fine-tuning and probing pipelines.

Significance is moderate: the modality gap is already well documented, and several competing mechanistic explanations exist (Liang et al. 2022; Levi and Gilboa 2025; Betser et al. 2025/2026); the paper articulates a complementary mechanism and motivates distributional diagnostics, but does not yet yield a new objective, algorithm, or sharp falsifiable prediction that practitioners can act on.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and carefully structured: the passage from stochastic InfoNCE to population partition fields, deterministic parametric energies, and intrinsic free-energy functionals is presented step by step with formal statements, proof intuitions, and complete proofs in the appendix (Theorems 3.1, 4.1 are proved with value- and gradient-consistency, using uniform gradient bounds in Lemma B.1/B.2 that appear correct).

The reframing of 'uniformity' as entropy acting as a tie-breaker within the alignment basin (Prop. 3.1, Prop. 3.2, Remark E.2) is an appealing conceptual contribution that offers a cleaner interpretation than the standard global alignment–uniformity trade-off story.

The diagnosis of the modality gap through a negative symmetric KL coupling between modality marginals (Def. 4.3, Prop. 4.1) is an interesting angle, and the explicit extremal construction in Prop. D.1 makes the coordinate-wise 'barrier' mechanism concrete and verifiable.

The limitations section (App. G.1) is honest and specific: it correctly identifies finite-temperature/finite-batch effects, the density-floor technicality, constant-kernel-volume homogeneity, and the absence of optimization dynamics as boundaries of the theory. The experimental appendices (F.1–F.4) provide enough procedural detail (seeds, sweep ranges, metrics) to support reasonable reproducibility of the synthetic studies.

The MS-COCO study of pretrained OpenCLIP checkpoints (Tab. 2, Figs. 6, 11) is a sensible empirical complement, showing that retrieval quality and distributional gap measures (energy distance, centroid gap) are related but non-identical.
weaknesses: The formal core is mathematically sound but largely predictable: Theorem 3.1's large-batch consistency reduces to a Hoeffding concentration argument plus standard differentiation-under-expectation, and Proposition 3.1 is a textbook Gibbs variational principle (the proof in App. C.2 is essentially the classical free-energy = KL identity). For a main-track theory paper, the depth of the genuinely new mathematics is modest.

The paper's central multimodal claim — that the cross-coupled geometry 'can sustain a persistent modality gap' — is never established at the level the narrative implies. Proposition 4.1 only characterizes the coordinate-wise infimum of a concave functional (a winner-take-all spike construction on the feasible set boundary); it does not prove existence, stability, or separation properties of minimizers of the joint functional, nor that trained encoders converge to separated marginals. The hedged 'can sustain' phrasing throughout (e.g., Punchline 2) reflects that the key qualitative bifurcation is asserted rather than proved.

The parametric inheritance results (Cor. E.1, E.2) largely assume their conclusion: Assumption E.1 and Eq. (69) posit that the encoder family can realize the intrinsic optimum up to a vanishing gap, which is precisely the hard part of connecting population geometry to actual neural training. As stated, these corollaries are conditional on an unverifiable expressivity premise rather than providing a bridge to practice.

There is a significant theory–practice gap that the experiments do not close: all theorems are pointwise in the parameters and the low-temperature limit is taken at fixed parameters, so the theory describes an objective's landscape, not what optimization reaches. The paper acknowledges this (G.1) but the abstract and introduction present population-level predictions as if validated; the experiments (synthetic particle surrogate, KDE-based training, linear encoders) only loosely corroborate qualitative trends.

The controlled MS-COCO intervention (caption corruption with frozen backbones, projection heads only) is a weak test of the theory: degrading positive-pair compatibility trivially degrades retrieval and plausibly widens marginal separation for many reasons, and no quantitative, theory-derived prediction (e.g., scaling of the gap with conditional heterogeneity) is tested against the data.

The analysis regime is quite restrictive: Assumption 2.1 (constant kernel volume) holds exactly only on homogeneous manifolds with cosine similarity; the Euclidean RBF regime used in one of the two main synthetic experiments does not satisfy it (App. A.1 concedes boundary corrections would change the clean identity), so even the numerical validation does not fully instantiate the stated theory.

The density floor (Def. 4.3) is a technical device, but the extremal 'spike' behavior in Prop. 4.1 is partly an artifact of the concave coordinate structure induced by the negative KL plus the floor; how this artificial boundary construction relates to finite-temperature learned densities is left unclear, weakening the force of the barrier narrative.

Related work on modality gap is discussed but the paper offers no comparative evaluation: it does not quantitatively contrast its mechanism with existing explanations (cone effect, dimension collapse, kernel-estimated divergence objectives such as Yin et al. 2026), so the reader cannot judge whether the divergence-coupling view explains the phenomenon better than prior accounts.

Given the hedged central claim, assumed expressivity, and illustrative rather than hypothesis-testing experiments, the significance of the contribution for practitioners (e.g., whether one should regularize cross-modal divergence and by how much) remains speculative.

strengths: The paper develops a clean and rigorous measure-theoretic framework connecting finite-batch InfoNCE to deterministic population energies, with both value and gradient consistency (Thms. 3.1, 4.1) proven under explicit, interpretable assumptions; the proofs in Apps. B-D are careful and largely correct, including uniform gradient bounds (Lem. B.1, B.2) and KDE-mismatch control under sharp kernels (Lem. B.3).

The unimodal analysis (strictly convex intrinsic free energy, unique Gibbs equilibrium Prop. 3.1, low-temperature concentration Prop. 3.2) is a satisfying reframing of 'uniformity' as entropic dispersion within the alignment basin, and the connection back to the parametric energy via the exact KL identity (Eq. 36) is elegant.

The multimodal bifurcation (Def. 4.3, Prop. 4.1) identifies a concrete mechanism — a negative symmetric KL coupling producing log-density barrier terms — that offers a plausible population-level explanation for the empirically observed CLIP modality gap, going beyond the alignment–uniformity picture.

The experimental design is layered sensibly: controlled synthetic checks of each theoretical ingredient (gradient consistency, Gibbs concentration, marginal gap under controlled misalignment), plus an intervention on MS-COCO (same-category caption corruption) that goes beyond a purely observational correlation with retrieval quality.

Assumptions, density floors, and regime boundaries (large-batch, low-temperature, homogeneous manifolds) are discussed honestly, and App. G contains a genuine limitations section covering finite-batch/temperature effects, singularities, and the gap between objective geometry and optimization dynamics.
weaknesses: The central multimodal claim is weaker than the framing suggests. Prop. 4.1 only shows the coordinate infimum is *approached* by degenerate, boundary-concentrating 'spike' densities; the functional is concave in each coordinate, so there is no minimizer and no characterization of actual stationary points or equilibria of the coupled two-modality system. The leap from 'the infimum is attained by extremal densities' to 'symmetric InfoNEC sustains a persistent modality gap under training' is a heuristic one; no dynamical or stationarity analysis bridges it (this is acknowledged in App. G.1 but remains the load-bearing gap).

The parametric inheritance results (Cor. E.1, E.2) rely on expressivity assumptions (Asm. E.1, Eq. 69) that essentially assume the encoder can realize the relevant intrinsic optimum up to vanishing error, together with vanishing energy-approximation errors along optimizing sequences. This makes the inheritance statements close to conditional restatements rather than substantive predictions.

The consistency theorems are pointwise in θ (and (θ,φ)), not uniform over parameter space, so their implications for optimization trajectories are limited; combined with the large-batch (N→∞) plus low-temperature (τ→0+) asymptotics, the analyzed regime is quite far from practical CLIP training (finite batches, τ≈0.07, and KDE smoothing replaced by encoder-induced structure).

Asm. 2.1 (constant kernel volume) holds exactly only on homogeneous manifolds such as the sphere; on generic compact domains the clean identity Γ=V_τ ρ̃ acquires position-dependent corrections. The experiments on compact Euclidean regimes (tanh encodings, RBF) therefore only 'test the mechanism numerically' rather than instantiate the theory, as the authors concede in App. F.1.

The MS-COCO caption-corruption experiment is consistent with the theory but not sharply discriminating: that weakening instance-level correspondence enlarges the marginal gap while degrading retrieval is also predicted by much coarser intuitions, and the experiment does not isolate the specific barrier/coupling mechanism (e.g., no measurement of the predicted effective field V12 or of conditional-law heterogeneity in real data). The observational study's non-monotonicity of gap vs. AvgR@1 is suggestive but involves only ~10 checkpoints.

Originality is solid but incremental relative to adjacent work: the large-batch limit argument is a comparatively standard concentration/dominated-convergence exercise, and variational/population-geometry analyses of contrastive objectives (e.g., Calder & Lee 2025) and modality-gap mechanisms (Liang et al. 2022; Levi & Gilboa 2025; Betser et al. 2025/2026) are an active area; the distinctive contribution is the negative-divergence coupling and its barrier interpretation, which rests on the caveats above.
